name: Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan)
short_status: Lost after a long eclipse in April 2022; ISRO declared it non-recoverable on 27 September 2022. First Asian spacecraft to orbit Mars, it arrived in September 2014 and worked eight years against a six-month design life.
tagline: ISRO · India · Orbiter · 2014 · The long occupation Ended
stats: Asian spacecraft to enter Mars orbit, and India's first interplanetary mission
ISRO's stated mission cost, about $80m in ISRO's own book and about $70m in NASA's catalogue
working at Mars against a six-month design life

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 5 November 2013 at 09:08 UTC (14:38 IST) on PSLV-C25 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. The rocket placed the spacecraft in a 250 by 23,550 km orbit of the Earth. That was not a Mars trajectory.

facts.label: Why six burns around the Earth
facts.value: The PSLV could not throw the spacecraft directly at Mars, so Mangalyaan raised its own apogee with six Earth-bound burns on 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 and 16 November 2013, working the apogee up from the 23,550 km of the launch orbit to 192,874 km before departure.

facts.label: The one that went wrong
facts.value: On 11 November 2013 the fourth burn delivered only 35 m/s instead of the planned 130 m/s, lifting apogee from 71,623 km to 78,276 km rather than about 100,000 km (ISRO's own log). An ISRO statement quoted the same day by The Planetary Society explained it: 'when both primary and redundant coils were energised together, as one of the planned modes, the flow to the Liquid Engine stopped.' ISRO's log records a supplementary burn on 12 November of 303.8 seconds, taking apogee from 78,276 km to 118,642 km.

facts.label: Trans-Mars injection
facts.value: 1 December 2013 at 00:49 IST, which is 30 November at 19:19 UTC. The liquid engine burned 1,328.89 seconds for 647.96 m/s. The spacecraft passed beyond Earth's sphere of influence at about 01:14 IST on 4 December 2013. Trajectory corrections followed on 11 December 2013 (40.5 seconds on the 22 N thrusters) and 11 June 2014 (16 seconds); a third, planned for August 2014, was not needed.

facts.label: Firsts, precisely
facts.value: MOM was the first Asian spacecraft to enter Mars orbit. Japan's Nozomi, launched in 1998, never made it: a valve failure at the December 1998 Earth swingby cost it the propellant margin, and after a four-year replanned trajectory the orbit insertion was abandoned in December 2003. China's Yinghuo-1 launched attached to Russia's Phobos-Grunt in November 2011 and never left Earth orbit. ISRO's own mission page describes it as having 'become the fourth space agency to successfully send a spacecraft to Mars orbit', after NASA, the Soviet programme and ESA.

facts.label: Waking the engine
facts.value: The 440 N liquid engine had sat unused for about 300 days, since the trans-Mars injection burn of 1 December 2013. On 22 September 2014 at 14:30 IST it was test-fired for 3.968 seconds, which doubled as the fourth trajectory correction, and ISRO reported the same day that it changed the spacecraft's velocity by 2.18 m/s. ISRO's briefing of 15 September had planned the burn at 3.968 seconds, 0.567 kg of propellant and 2.142 m/s.

facts.label: Mars orbit insertion
facts.value: 24 September 2014. The burn began at 07:17:32 IST, which is 01:47:32 UTC, using the 440 N engine plus eight 22 N thrusters. Planned duration 1,454 seconds (24 minutes 14 seconds), 249.5 kg of propellant, 1,098.7 m/s. The spacecraft went into eclipse five minutes before ignition and behind Mars four minutes after it, so the confirmation reached Earth partway through. ISRO announced afterwards that the burn had lasted 1,388.67 seconds and changed the velocity by 1,099 m/s.

facts.label: The orbit, which sources disagree about
facts.value: ISRO's pre-insertion briefing targeted 423 by 80,000 km with a 3.2-day period. ISRO's announcement on the day of arrival gave the orbit achieved as 421.7 by 76,993.6 km, inclination 150 degrees, period 72 hours 51 minutes 51 seconds, and the trajectory JPL reconstructed from tracking, served through its Horizons system, agrees with it closely. NSSDCA's catalogue, and the descriptive notes of that same Horizons record, instead give 366 by 80,000 km and 76.7 hours, a period close to the 3.2-day target. In June 2015 ISRO's 100th-orbit page gave the working orbit as 474 by 71,132 km. The briefing figure is a target, the September 2014 figure is the orbit achieved, and the June 2015 figure is the orbit as it stood nine months later.

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: 1,340 kg at launch of which 852 kg was propellant, leaving 488 kg dry. A roughly 1.5 m cube on a modified IRS/INSAT/Chandrayaan-1 bus, one three-panel solar wing giving 800 W at Mars, a 36 amp-hour lithium-ion battery, a 2.2 m S-band high-gain antenna, and a 440 N bipropellant main engine.

facts.label: Payload
facts.value: 15 kg in five instruments: Mars Colour Camera, Thermal Infrared Imaging Spectrometer, Methane Sensor for Mars, Lyman Alpha Photometer and Mars Exospheric Neutral Composition Analyser. For comparison, MAVEN, which arrived two days earlier, carried 65 kg of instruments.

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: ISRO gives the mission as 'Rupees 450 Cr' (4.5 billion rupees). ISRO's own illustrated book converts that to 'about 80 million American Dollars'; NASA's NSSDCA converts the same rupee figure to '$70 million contemporaneous US'; press coverage of the 2022 end of mission used $74 million. These are one rupee number at different exchange rates. None of them is a competing cost estimate.

facts.label: Design life and longevity
facts.value: The design mission life was six months, which ISRO's 100th-orbit page records as 'completed on March 24, 2015'. MOM reached its 100th Mars orbit in June 2015 and 1,000 Earth days in orbit on 19 June 2017, which ISRO recorded as 973.24 Martian sols and 388 orbits.

facts.label: The eclipse it dodged
facts.value: An eclipse of up to 8 hours was coming, against a battery designed for about 1 hour 40 minutes. On 17 January 2017 all eight 22 N thrusters fired for 431 seconds for 97.5 m/s, moving the orbit so that the eclipse duration fell to zero through September 2017. ISRO recorded that this used about 20 kg of propellant, 'leaving another 13 kg of propellant for its further mission life.'

facts.label: The end
facts.value: ISRO states that MOM lost communication with the ground station 'as a result of a long eclipse in April 2022', that the propellant 'must have been exhausted' so the spacecraft could not hold the attitude needed for sustained power generation, and that at the national meet of 27 September 2022 'it was declared that the spacecraft is non-recoverable, and attained its end-of-life.' ISRO has not published a precise date for the loss of contact.

facts.label: The methane sensor
facts.value: ISRO's payload page still says the Methane Sensor for Mars 'can measure CH4 concentration in the Martian atmosphere with few parts-per-billion accuracy'. The instrument team's own paper gives its methane sensitivity as 38 to 60 ppb for a 10 second integration and its measurement accuracy as 30 to 65 ppb at 10 seconds and 30 per cent scene reflectance, against a Martian methane abundance the same paper's introduction puts near 10 ppb on average. The same paper adds that 'accuracy can be further enhanced by increasing the data integration time', so the figures are a performance estimate at one setting that longer integration can improve. ISRO's 1000-days-in-orbit page later reported that 'though MSM could not detect any methane (above its sensitivity limit), it provided excellent reflectance data of Mars surface', and the data was published as a short-wave infrared albedo map.

facts.label: Output
facts.value: ISRO's own publications list ran to 27 entries in September 2019; reading it, roughly half describe the spacecraft, the launch vehicle, the instruments or mission operations rather than results derived from Mars data. ISRO's current page says the Mars Colour Camera 'has produced 1100+ images so far' and that the mission 'published more than 35 research papers in peer-reviewed journals'.

timeline: PSLV-C25 launches Mangalyaan at 09:08 UTC into a 250 by 23,550 km Earth orbit. India's first interplanetary launch.

Six Earth-bound burns raise apogee. The fourth, on 11 November, underperforms when primary and redundant valve coils are energised together and fuel flow stops; a supplementary burn the next day recovers it.
Trans-Mars injection at 00:49 IST (30 November 19:19 UTC), a 1,328.89 second burn for 647.96 m/s. Earth's sphere of influence is left on 4 December.
First trajectory correction, 40.5 seconds on the 22 N thrusters, with the spacecraft 2.9 million km from Earth.
The main engine is test-fired for 3.968 seconds after roughly 300 idle days, doubling as the final trajectory correction.

Mars orbit insertion. The burn starts at 01:47:32 UTC (07:17:32 IST) and runs 1,388.67 seconds, about 23 minutes. ISRO becomes the fourth space agency to put a spacecraft in Mars orbit, two days after MAVEN.
The Mars Colour Camera photographs Phobos and, from outside Deimos's orbit, the anti-Mars side of Deimos at about 300 m per pixel.
The six-month design mission life is completed. Everything after this is bonus time.
ISRO releases a scientific Mars atlas built from Mars Colour Camera imagery.
Eight thrusters fire for 431 seconds, 97.5 m/s, to reduce an impending 8 hour eclipse to zero. It costs about 20 kg of propellant and leaves roughly 13 kg.
A long eclipse arrives with no propellant left to avoid it. The spacecraft cannot hold the attitude needed to recharge, and contact is lost.
At a national meet marking eight years in orbit, ISRO declares the spacecraft non-recoverable and at the end of its life.
